rows.q: Katz says there is no economy. A sceptical economist replies that markets obviously coordinate millions of decisions with no center at all. How would Katz answer, and where is his answer weakest?
rows.a:
## What "no economy" claims

The slogan is easy to misread as a denial that markets coordinate anything. It is a claim about what markets are and what they rest on. In its strongest form:

> "There is no 'economy.' There is only, as there always has been, ritual distribution from the center." ([Will Have Been the Same](/post/will-have-been-the-same-future-perfectism-or-derivatives-of-the-tributary#p-1))

"The economy" here means the economist's object: a self-standing sphere of individual choices that spontaneously produces order and that politics then "regulates" from outside. Katz says that object is an abstraction from something prior, which is distribution and the debt every participant owes to whatever center distributes and protects. The joint essay with Zack Baker frames it as our "originary debt to the center" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-95)).

He is not anti-market, and he is not an economic reductionist in reverse. In an early post he objects to taking any one economy as the model for all: "There are many economies and they supplement and supplant each other in many ways" ([Economism](/post/economism#p-3)).

## How Katz would answer the economist

**1. He accepts Hayek's point and then moves it.** Katz does not dispute that distributed knowledge can't be gathered in one planning office. The Hayekian counter "is true as far as it goes. Every point of decision making is irreducible and the authority needed to make each decision is to be respected. But the center need not be thought of as a planning center" ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-3)). The economist's argument runs together *decentralized decision* and *no center*. Katz keeps the first and rejects the second. He compares it to a general: subordinates must improvise because no general can foresee every contingency, and "There will therefore be 'markets' all along the line" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-13)). Leeway is something authority grants and bounds. It is not evidence that authority is absent.

**2. The market is a capillary region.** His working definition is "what people without direct authority for maintaining the social center do with knowledge, information and skills when they are being protected and bounded but not directly supervised by such authorities" ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-1)). Read as an ontology of free choices, the standard picture is "absurd, if for no other reason than that no one chooses the language in which these choices are made" (same paragraph). The economist's "millions of decisions" are real, but they take place inside conditions no participant decided: property titles, enforceable contracts, a currency, protection from violence. Katz asks the businessman whether he could defend himself "against violence, fraud, robbery and extortion" without the state. Then he notes that liberal theory nonetheless treats the state as a hired "Pinkertons" called in after a peaceful exchange order already existed ([Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog#p-15)).

**3. Markets are made, and money issues from the center.** On the historical side: "Markets do not spring up spontaneously out of an evolving division of labor... Markets are created by states so as to provision their militaries when abroad" ([Center and Distribution](/post/anthropomorphics-center-and-distribution#p-2)). Drawing on Colin Drumm, Katz adds that even an ordinary market needs someone standing behind it: "something like a 'lender of last resort' is constitutive of any market" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-62)). In 2008 the economist's centerless order was saved by a central bank. That is Katz's point.

**4. Large-scale coordination already looks less like a market.** Big firms coordinate through supply chains, long-term contracts and near-monopolies, not spot prices. Katz therefore argues "how close we already are to a planned global economy" through those chains ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-18)), with the free market surviving "only at the margins."

## Where the answer is weakest

**1. It establishes preconditions and then claims more.** A careful economist can grant every point: markets were created by states, require courts and money, and depend on a lender of last resort. That economist can still say that within those conditions the allocation of steel, labour and bread is coordinated by prices that no one at the center sets or could set. Showing where something came from does not show how it operates now. Katz half-concedes this in a striking passage: "There will be all kinds of 'interfaces' where the market rules in the sense a liberal economist means. It may be that majority, even the vast majority, of transactions take place at such interfaces" ([What are We Talking About](/post/what-are-we-talking-about-when-we-talk-about-the-market-gablog#p-16)). If most transactions are market-ruled, "there is no economy" reduces to a claim about framing and dependence. That claim is defensible, but it is much weaker than the slogan.

**2. The price problem is named but not solved.** Katz says so directly: "This brings us up against the notorious pricing problem, which is taken to be the doom of non-capitalistic systems" ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-16)). His proposed replacements include publicly ranked successors whose "constant fluctuations in succession replicate price change" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)), "controlled usurpations" between firms in a supply chain ([Monopoly](/post/monopoly#p-21)), and machine learning on large datasets. All of these are much coarser signals than millions of prices adjusting continuously. He is candid about this elsewhere: "if that's utopian, so be it" ([Can Networks Crowd Out Markets?](/post/can-networks-crowd-out-markets-gablog#p-5)). This is where an economist would push hardest, and fairly.

**3. The concept of the center can stretch to cover anything.** In the data-economy essays the center becomes "whatever will turn out to have been furthest upstream" of all data flows ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-5)). If the center is simply whatever stands upstream of a process, then no market can count as centerless, because by definition it has an upstream. That protects the thesis, but it risks making it unfalsifiable. The economist can fairly ask what observation would show that a given coordination had no center in Katz's sense.

The strongest form of Katz's reply is the moderate one: decentralized decision is real, but it is a delegation within a protected order and not a counterexample to centrality. The question that stays open is the economist's original one: who sets the price of bricks?

**To read next:** [Market Capillarism](/post/market-capillarism-gablog), the clearest statement of the "capillary" definition. [Monopoly](/post/monopoly), where Katz takes on the pricing problem directly.

A test you could try: pick an ordinary price, say rent in your city, and trace it back. Which parts of it are set by distribution from some authority (zoning, credit, title), and which by bargaining that nobody directs? Where you draw that line is where your agreement or disagreement with Katz lies.

rows.q: I run a 40-person company and two senior people are fighting over who leads a new product. Use imperative exchange, the pointman and succession to tell me what to do on Monday.
rows.a:
Katz doesn't write management advice, but he insists these concepts apply at every scale: "Each institution has a head, and this head has an appointed successor, and the successor has an appointed successor, all the way down through each institution" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-16)). So this applies the theory to your case. It is not a passage where he takes up your situation.

## First, see what the fight actually is

It looks like two peers quarrelling. In Center Study's terms it is two petitions addressed to you. Katz holds that "all desires (I want this, I want that) can be constructed as imperatives directed to some center," a center from which the desirer expects commands in return, "upon obedience to which compliance with the petitioner's request will be contingent (the imperative exchange)" ([Moral Thresholds](/post/moral-thresholds#p-3)). Each of them is in effect saying: *I have done what this company asked of me; now give me this.* The rivalry between them is downstream of that. They are fighting each other because the center, which is you, hasn't spoken.

That also tells you why the fight is dangerous. Katz on succession: "if you are not choosing your successor you are not actually in power, because everyone around you can hedge on various degrees of obedience and support by transferring promises of obedience and support to the more likely successors" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)). The same logic holds at the scale of a product lead. While the question stays open, people beneath these two will start hedging, attaching themselves to whoever looks likelier to win. The open question is itself what is splitting the team.

## The pointman's job

Katz chose "pointman" for the occupant of the center because the role is double: "He is at the point, taking the initiative, gathering all initiatives under his banner, and at the same time the one everyone points to" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-16)). You can't step out of that by handing the decision to a committee, a vote, or "let them work it out." Each of those just hides the center. Then the resentment has nowhere legible to go, and it settles on the two people themselves.

## Monday, concretely

**1. Hear each of them once, and steer the conversation toward requests rather than demands.** Katz's model of the mature imperative exchange is the petition that has become "Tell me how to do what you are telling me to do" ([Media, Technology and Originary Grammar](/post/media-technology-and-originary-grammar#p-20)). Don't ask "why should it be you?", because that invites a campaign speech against the rival. Ask each one: *If you led this, what would you need from me, and what would you need from the other person?* The answers are your data. Watch which of them can describe a place for the other.

**2. Decide yourself, and name an order, not just a winner.** Centered ordinality means someone goes first, someone second, and so on. Appoint the lead, and in the same move name the other person's position relative to that lead, in plain words. Katz's later proposal has every head "publicly choosing their successor and even ranking possible successors" ([Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-6)). Applied here, the loser has a ranked place, not an exit.

**3. Make the decision revisable, and say so.** In Katz's scheme the selection "would not be made once and for all"; conditions change and candidates "reveal themselves in new ways" ([The Sufficiency…](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-8)). This isn't softening the blow. It tells both of them that the center keeps watching, which gives the second person a reason to perform rather than sulk.

**4. Give the lead the power the job requires.** "It is immoral to give someone responsibility for doing something without giving them the power to do it" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-61)). If the new lead has the title but the other person keeps a veto over hiring, budget, or the roadmap, you haven't decided anything. You've moved the fight downstairs. Co-leadership is the most likely version of this mistake.

**5. Deal with the resentment directly.** Katz defines resentment as "your fulfilling of an imperative, having the reciprocal imperative you issue go unfulfilled, while not letting that reciprocal imperative lapse" ([Resentment](/post/resentment#p-19)). The person who loses will feel they kept their side of an exchange and you didn't keep yours. So ask them, privately, what they believe they were owed. Then either honor it some other way, or tell them clearly that it isn't owed. Doing that lets the claim lapse, which is how Katz defines forgiveness.

## The question underneath

Succession "in perpetuity" means you aren't only picking the best person for this product. You're asking who will be best at choosing *their* successor. Of your two senior people, which one is building people beneath them? That is a better tiebreaker than which of them argues more forcefully.

**To read next:** [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity) for why choosing is the proof of power, and [Resentment](/post/resentment) for handling the person who loses.

A question for you: before Monday, can you say what imperative each of them believes they have already fulfilled for you? Whoever can't answer that clearly is probably not the one to lead.

rows.q: Explain how the ostensive, imperative and declarative relate to Katz's account of money as debt to the center, for someone who knows Girard well but has never read Gans.
rows.a:
## Where Gans departs from Girard

Start from what you already know. In Girard, mimetic rivalry escalates into a war of all against all, the crisis discharges onto a single victim, and the victim becomes the god. Gans, whom Katz follows here, keeps the mimetic crisis but objects that a killing by itself founds nothing: "there's no reason why some animal group, even an exceptionally intelligent one, should view ganging up on and killing one of its members as 'meaningful,' which is to say, 'memorable'" ([Event, Origin, Center](/post/event-origin-center#p-38)).

What is missing is a **sign**. Gans moves the crisis onto an object, "most likely some food source, perhaps a recent kill" ([Origin and Hypothesis](/post/anthropomorphics-origin-and-hypothesis#p-4)). Everyone converges on it. Then someone hesitates, and their reach becomes a pointing, an *aborted gesture of appropriation*. The others imitate it. The object becomes the **center**: sacred because it held everyone back, desirable because everyone wants it. No murder is required. For Katz the important thing is the **deferral** of violence, not its discharge.

That first sign is the **ostensive**: a pointing or naming that works only when its object is present.

## How the speech forms grow out of mistakes

Gans then derives the other speech forms from the ostensive. Each one appears when the previous form fails, and the failure is repaired instead of punished. As Katz puts it, "the mistake is not corrected but 'completed' and thereby changed into a new kind of sign" ([Originary Mistakenness](/post/anthropoetics-originary-mistakenness#p-18)).

- **Imperative.** Someone names an object that isn't there, an "inappropriate ostensive." Another person fetches it to rescue the sign. Nobody set out to issue a command, but one now exists ([Felicity](/post/felicity#p-10)).
- **Interrogative.** An imperative can't be fulfilled. Rather than escalate, it softens into a request for information.
- **Declarative.** The object cannot be supplied. The answer repeats its name together with a "don't." Katz reads this "operator of interdiction" as two imperatives at once. The one making the demand is told to stop, and the object itself has been ordered away, a command that can only come from the center: "the imperator is told to cease and desist 'because' the object has been ordered away" ([Felicity](/post/felicity#p-19)).

The declarative creates "reality": a world that refuses our demands under authority that belongs to none of us. This is Katz's addition to Gans, the "bidirectional imperative" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-7)).

## Imperative exchange: the hinge to debt

In ritual, the community and the center trade imperatives. The god commands an offering, and the worshippers petition the god to keep providing. Katz calls this **imperative exchange**. When the exchange fails (the rains don't come), the community narrates what went wrong at the center, and that narration is myth ([Programming, Power and Declarative Culture](/post/programming-power-and-declarative-culture#p-3)).

The trade is never symmetrical. The center gave first: it created the community by sparing it. So the human condition is already a **debt to the center**, and every imperative carries an account. "An imperative, whether it be a command, demand or anything in between, always looks forward to some exchange" ([Credit-Idiom-Imperative Perfection](/post/credit-idiom-imperative-perfection-expectant-scenes#p-6)).

## Money as the extension of that debt

Once a human (the Big Man, then the king, then the emperor) occupies the ritual center, the community no longer settles its debt in one shared sacrificial meal. Distribution passes through layers of delegates, and money comes in to stretch the scene across distance and time. Katz quotes Gans's definition of money as "a credit drawn on the sacred that cannot be freely reproduced," and builds on Christine Desan's history: "Money records, by the center, a debt paid to the center" ([There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-8), [#p-36](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-36)).

The coin is a token the center hands out and later accepts back in place of a contribution. Markets are not spontaneous barter either; they "represent forms of delegation by the central authority" ([The Generativity of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-the-generativity-of-the-center#p-17)). So money does not measure some intrinsic value. It "measures the relation someone with some amount of it at a given moment has with debt enforcing and money issuing institutions" ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-31)).

Mapped onto the grammar:

- **Ostensive.** The coin is a designated token that points back to a center. Its value consists in being recognized as the same token by everyone.
- **Imperative.** Debt is a command that is not yet fulfilled. Enforcement and forgiveness are the center's choices about which commands to collect.
- **Declarative.** Credit has the structure of the declarative. A present demand is deferred against a reality guaranteed elsewhere, at a later time, by an authority none of the parties controls. Katz says this directly: "to speak in sentences is to draw upon and issue lines of credit" ([Tokenizing Deferrality](/post/tokenizing-deferrality#p-8)). In the same way, "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud…](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)).

## What a Girardian should notice

In Girard, the economy of exchange is an aftereffect of the sacrifice. In Katz, exchange is the sacrificial relation itself, made explicit and spread across a whole society. Modern finance remains a ritual of indebtedness: the "economy" functions as a metaperson whose will we try to discern, and the central bank becomes the lender of last resort ([There Is No Economy](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf#p-44)). Katz's political project follows from this. If debt is originary, the goal is not to abolish it, as anarchists like Graeber would. The goal is to clarify it, by tying credit to succession and to adjudicable judgment. He even proposes the "sample" as an emissary "that we now preserve and amplify rather than sacrificing" ([Lecture 5: The Sign](/post/the-sign-pdf#p-19)). That is his answer to the victim at the center of Girard's scene.

## Read next

- [There Is No Economy but Only the Debt to the Center](/post/there-is-no-economy-pdf) is the full argument on money, Desan, Drumm's "outside spread," and derivatives as ritual.
- [Felicity](/post/felicity) is Katz's clearest step-by-step account of how imperative and declarative emerge.

An exercise to try: take a mortgage and describe it purely in these terms. What is pointed to, what is commanded, and by whom? Which authority guarantees the "reality" in which the debt will be paid?

rows.q: What exactly is idiomclining, how is it different from coining jargon, and can you idiomcline this sentence of mine: "Our team needs better communication"?
rows.a:
## What idiomclining is

The word is Katz's coinage, built from his older term "upclining." He takes it from linguists' work on *grammaticization*: words tend to slide along a "cline" from full meaning toward pure grammatical function. "Take" starts as something you do with your hands and ends up in "take responsibility," "take time," "take over." His project was to run that slide in reverse, "retrieving grammaticized signs and re-semanticizing them" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-16)). In his earlier essay he describes an upcline as a move "in which a word is deliberately removed from a circulation that splinters its uses, and placed within a new circulation, or idiom, that treats the word as a prompt for a new hierarchy of declaratives, imperatives and ostensives" ([Attentionality and Originary Ethics](/post/attentionality-originary-ethics#p-49)). His model case is Plato pulling "good" out of everyday use (a good baker, a good meal) and turning it into *the Good*.

"Idiomclining" widens this into a general way of working with language:

> "dedicating oneself to setting relatively immobilized 'pieces' of language back into motion seems a good way of thinking about operating within an idiom. You will always be mistaken in doing so, precisely because you'll be violating some convention or expectation, but you also can't go wrong because you present a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others" ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-17))

He offers it as a replacement for "'critical thinking' or other bureaucratized categories designed for mass test taking." It is "a more semiotic way of speaking about stopping and thinking before doing as itself a kind of doing." The method is conversion and compression: "moving through and translating the other idioms so as to derive imperatives out of declaratives and ostensives out of imperatives" ([p-18](/post/idiomclining#p-18)).

Those last terms come from what Katz calls *originary grammar*. An **ostensive** points: *that, there.* An **imperative** demands: *do this.* A **declarative** states: *this is the case.* Idiomclining takes a frozen statement and works back down that chain. What is it really asking someone to do? What would we point to once it was done? The aim, in his words, is to make your idiom "both more idiomatic and more transferable" ([p-15](/post/idiomclining#p-15)). It should be sharp enough to belong to this scene and portable enough to start new exchanges elsewhere.

## How it differs from coining jargon

The question is fair, because Katz does coin a lot of terms and defends specialized vocabulary. He argues that what looks like jargon "is very often a way of phrasing some claim that has resulted from the cumulative responses to attacks on a dozen previous ways of phrasing it" ([The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-4)). So the line between the two is not whether a word is unfamiliar. It is which direction the word moves.

**Jargon freezes.** Drawing on Alice Becker-Ho, Katz notes that jargon's aim "is to come across as a specialist." It "serves more to mark out a distance than to set up a real barrier," "protecting the privileges of a caste" ([Book Review: The Essence of Jargon](/post/double-helix-v4-becker-ho-review#p-10)). His own diagnosis is grammatical. Nouns made out of verbs ("nominalizations") can "freeze discourse into jargon," and the cure is "refusing the imperatives the nominalizations start giving you, the imperative exchanges they lure you into (the belief that this terminological tweak with solve the problem)" ([Technology and Magic, Doings and Happenings](/post/technology-and-magic-doings-and-happenings#p-21)).

**Idiomclining unfreezes.** It takes the frozen noun and asks who is doing what, at whose command, toward what. Jargon is a badge you wear. An idiomclined phrase is a tool you hand to someone. You give them a term they can use and test, which may change it.

## Your sentence: "Our team needs better communication"

This is close to the textbook case. Katz specifically lists "communication" among the words he distrusts ([Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining#p-1)). Here is the treatment, step by step.

**1. Diagnose.** "Communication" is a nominalization that hides who says what to whom. "Better" is an assessment that gives no instruction. Katz says something similar of writing teachers who tell students to be "clear": such terms "allow us to assess... but they tell us nothing about how the writing was produced" ([The Meaning of Meaning](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage#p-13)). "Needs" is an imperative addressed to nobody. The sentence is a complaint posing as a diagnosis. It invites "the belief that this terminological tweak will solve the problem."

**2. Find the scene and the center.** Every team has a center: a captain, a shared task, something its attention converges on ([Hostages, Proxies, and Moles](/post/hostages-proxies-and-moles#p-5)). Behind the sentence there must be a specific failure. A command got lost between being given and being carried out. Someone acted on a decision nobody else knew had been made. Katz calls this the *imperative gap*: the difference between the command issued and the command obeyed. "Better communication" is the name people give to that gap when they don't want to say whose command fell into it.

**3. Lower it to plain words.** Katz sometimes tests a phrase by restating it in Anna Wierzbicka's "primes," the handful of words found in every language. In those terms: *someone in our team says something; other people in our team don't know it; because of this, they do something bad.* This is already more useful than the original, because each clause points somewhere you could look.

**4. Recover the imperative and the ostensive.** What is the command, and what would we point to once it had been obeyed? Here are some candidate idiomclinings, each aiming at a different possible gap:

- *"Say it back before you do it."* After any instruction, the person carrying it out restates it in their own words. The ostensive is the restatement itself, heard by both people.
- *"Every decision has a name and an owner."* When something is decided, it gets a short name and a person who answers for it. You can then point at the list.
- *"Anyone should be able to say what the captain wants this week, in the same words."* This tests whether the center's command actually reaches the edges of the team.

Each is in the present tense, gives an instruction, and can be checked. Each is also portable: another team could pick it up and alter it. That is the "more idiomatic and more transferable" double movement.

**5. Admit the mistakenness.** I don't know your team, so all three may miss the actual failure. On Katz's terms that is fine, because the attempt "present[s] a opportunity for an adjusted response on the part of others." Put one to the team and watch which part they object to. The objection is where the real gap is.

## Where to read next

- [Idiomclining](/post/idiomclining) is the source essay, short and dense. Read it for the link between idiom, deferral, and the "safely buffered" scenes where play with language becomes possible.
- [The Meaning of Meaning, and Metalanguage](/post/the-meaning-of-meaning-and-metalanguage) explains why words like "clear," "communication," and "rights" assess without instructing. Its last paragraphs give a practical method: "use the words others mention, and mention the words others use."

An exercise to try: what was the specific moment that made someone say "we need better communication"? Write that moment as a single present-tense sentence with a named person in it. Then idiomcline that sentence instead of the abstraction.

rows.q: Trace how the concept of the center changes from Anthropomorphics to the recent essays on thirdness and data exchange. What stayed, and what was dropped?
rows.a:
Katz never threw the center out. The structure built in *Anthropomorphics* (2019) survives almost entire. What changes is what the center is made of, which institution stands between it and everyone else, and how its occupant can be held to account. Here is the trajectory as the texts show it.

## 1. The center in *Anthropomorphics*: two centers and a gap

The book's basic distinction is between the **signifying center**, the paradoxical object or being that commands deferral (ultimately God, or "reality"), and the **occupied center**, the human who has held that place since the Big Man took it. The book's whole political problem lives in the gap between them:

> "There is, in any community, a central authority, the final source of imperatives; and yet those imperatives are only worthy of being followed if the central authority is in accord with the signifying center" ([The Center and Imperative Authority](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-and-imperative-authority#p-1))

Three things fill that gap in the book:

- **Imperative exchange.** We obey the center and petition it in return, and prayer is the model.
- **The disciplines.** They work in the "imperative gap" between a command issued and a command obeyed, and send feedback upward without appealing to any "super-sovereign."
- **Naming.** The sovereign is in effect "onomastician-in-chief," and naming places a thing "under the authority of the broader system of signs" ([Maintaining the Present of the Center](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-35)).

Succession is already the decisive question: "The solution I propose: the current occupant of the center chooses his successor" ([same text, p-2](/post/anthropomorphics-maintaining-the-present-of-the-center#p-2)). The posture toward that occupant is strict: "What is absolutely forbidden under such an order is directing violent centralization toward the authorities" ([The Center, Speaking](/post/anthropomorphics-the-center-speaking#p-13)). The center here is above all a *speaker* that we learn to hear. The book ends on "the center speaking to itself" through us.

## 2. What stayed

Nearly all of this survives:

- **The center precedes the margin.** The originary claim that "we are created by the thing at the center" never wavers. The 2025 essay on the name *Anthropomorphics* restates it: "we were always already imitating the center that was itself nothing more than a vectorization of our converging desires turned back at us through a prohibition" ([Anthropomorphics](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)).
- **The two centers.** Katz keeps returning to "the problem of the two centers." By 2024 he resolves it by saying that the "centripetal" centers that empire produces "draw our attention away from the social center towards samples," and that serving the center now means curating those samples ([Learncoin](/post/learncoin#p-3)).
- **Succession.** It is radicalized rather than dropped. It becomes *singularized succession in perpetuity*, choosing "someone who will in turn select someone who will in turn select someone, etc." ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-3)).
- **Imperative grammar.** The ostensive-imperative-interrogative-declarative sequence becomes the frame for technology itself ("the perfection of the imperative") and for media.
- **Donating resentment to the center.** The formula stays and gets sharpened: "The center doesn't resent—that would serve as a definition of the center" ([The Tokenization of Resentment](/post/the-tokenization-of-resentment#p-15)).

## 3. What changed

**(a) The center becomes infrastructural, a "central intelligence."** In the book the center is primarily a person and a sacred locus. In the data essays it becomes a position in the flow of information:

> "the center is whatever will turn out to have been furthest upstream of that" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-5))

> "The center is now the entire data infrastructure and its algorithmic treatments that one must donate to and extract from: the central intelligence." ([Centrifugal Signifying](/post/centrifugal-signifying#p-21))

Correspondingly, sovereignty is imagined as falling to whichever data-security firm attains "a temporary monopoly on treating data for purposes of judgment" ([A New Model of Power](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-15)).

**(b) Exchange becomes debt and data.** Imperative exchange is reworked as originary debt: "we're all indebted to the center—this is originary, not modern, but what is modern is that the value of our debt is determined by expectation of future earnings" ([Debt and the Stack](/post/debt-and-the-stack#p-4)). Thirdness then asks that every conflict be refigured as "each party donating and/or receiving data from the center in lieu of such things as punishment or damages" ([Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-2)). Petitioning the center becomes supplying it with well-curated data. You present yourself as a *sample*.

**(c) The juridical replaces the disciplines as the chief mediator.** In the book the disciplines fill the imperative gap. In the Thirdness essays the juridical is "a kind of irreducible, if less originary, middle term between ritual (originary distribution) and the disciplinary" ([Modeling Thirdness, p-1](/post/modeling-thirdness#p-1)). It sits between the vendetta from below and the "antinomic" vendetta against the nomos from above. Power itself is redefined: "all power is exercised through judgments" ([A New Model of Power, p-3](/post/a-new-model-of-power#p-3)). Note the self-cancelling horizon this adds, which the book did not have: "The perfection of the juridical would then be its abolition" ([If… Then](/post/if-then-the-idiom-of-data-exchange-substack#p-4)).

**(d) The occupant can now be put on trial.** This is the sharpest reversal of tone. In place of the book's flat prohibition, the 2025 essays build the risk into a ritual: "in place of the sacrifice of the central figure we have the high stakes lawsuit against him" ([The Pointman](/post/the-pointman#p-19)), with countersuit as the guard ("if you want to charge the king with treason be prepared to be charged with it yourself" ([Thirdness and the Same Sentence](/post/thirdness-and-the-same-sentence#p-16))).

**(e) The occupant is renamed and made more mobile.** "Sovereign" and "occupant of the center" give way to "pointman" and even "dictator." The model of succession also changes. In the book, top-tier candidates were kept out of real power to suppress rivalry. Now succession is meant to *fluctuate* openly, ranked lists revised like prices, until it replaces the market ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-13); [Originary Debt, Credit, Succession](/post/originary-debt-credit-succession#p-6)).

## 4. What was dropped, or receded

Little is renounced outright, so here I am reading drift more than stated retractions:

- **The flat ban on accusing the occupant** gives way to the lawsuit model above.
- **"Rights" and "super-sovereignty" as the main enemy concepts** recede. The target shifts to the oscillation between central bank and central intelligence (the "outside spread" and the "outside option," terms he borrows from Colin Drumm).
- **The name itself.** Katz says he "settled instead on the more disciplinary sounding 'center study'" ([Anthropomorphics, p-2](/post/anthropomorphics-substack#p-2)). Anthropomorphics returns later as the *design* side of the same Möbius strip.
- **Onomastics as the sovereign's signature act.** It doesn't vanish, but naming is now folded into labeling and curating data, together with "idiom mining."

## Where to read next

- [Modeling Thirdness](/post/modeling-thirdness): the clearest statement of the juridical turn and of data exchange "in lieu of" punishment.
- [The Pointman](/post/the-pointman): shows how the sacrificial logic Katz analyzed in *Anthropomorphics* is converted into the lawsuit-and-succession ritual.

An exercise: take the book's line that imperatives are "only worthy of being followed if the central authority is in accord with the signifying center," and ask what the *signifying* center becomes once the center is "the entire data infrastructure." Is there still a gap between the two centers, or has curating samples closed it?

rows.q: On Katz's account, why can a language model write fluent declaratives but not promise or deem? Does that argument hold up?
rows.a:
## The argument

The starting point is Katz's grammar. In the line of speech forms that runs from the ostensive through the imperative and the interrogative to the declarative, the declarative comes last and is derivative. It is a deferred imperative that points to an object that isn't present. Writing then lifts the declarative out of the ostensive and imperative world and treats it as the primary form of language. Olson's "metalanguage of literacy" names that move, and Katz's word for its hypostasis is "metaphysics." A language model trained on text is in effect a machine built from that declarative order. It can produce well-formed declaratives indefinitely because declaratives were designed to circulate apart from any particular speaker on any particular scene.

Promises and deemings sit at the other end of the grammar. Katz groups them on purpose:

"Deeming is part of a cluster of other words and phrases in the ostensive-imperative-ostensive sphere that become especially important within the Stack because uncannily similar to programming: promise, prayer, oath, curse, bless, oblige, thank, grace" ([Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-13))

These are performatives. They don't describe a state of affairs. They place the speaker in what Katz calls "the chain of originary debt to the center" (same passage). To promise is to take on a debt: "A promise draws credit from the promisee and places one in debt" ([Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-10)). To deem is to name something as what it is, and that is a form of authority. The passage that carries the most weight is this one:

"promising, indebting, and issuing credit are speech acts that cannot be reduced to computation, and are therefore the domain of decision. (A promise includes an articulation of predictions… but in both cases broader conditions of predictability are necessary for these more localized predictions to be possible and those broader conditions require humans to be reliable before they are predictable.)" ([Promise, Fraud…](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah#p-12))

So the point isn't that a model lacks some inner capacity. A promise only means something if someone can be held to it: someone who stands on the scene, can default, and can be enforced against or forgiven. Elsewhere Katz says every utterance carries an element of promise, and its meaning lies in "how well we can know what the conditions… will be like when the debt comes due" ([All You Need Is Language](/post/all-you-need-is-language#p-12)). A model can predict what a promiser would say. It can't be the debtor. And deeming carried out by an algorithm is acceptable only if the algorithm has itself "been authorized or deemed worthy to do so, by, ultimately, a human" ([Toward a Curriculum…](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-12)).

Beneath that is the deeper claim: "All that differentiates us fundamentally from the machines… is deferral—the deferral of appropriation" ([Brute Force Computation and the Debt to the Center](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-23)). A promise defers: I hold back my present freedom for a future obligation. A model has no appropriation to defer and no mimetic rivalry it is restraining. So it has nothing at stake in the sign, and the promise has nothing to bind.

## Does it hold up?

I think it is strong in one form and weak in another, and Katz himself marks the weak one.

**The strong form concerns standing, not detection.** Read as a claim that a promise requires a party who is accountable within a structure of debt and enforcement, the argument is persuasive. It also fits his wider position that a juridical order needs someone who can be put in the dock. The critical test is a model's "promise" that a deployer has committed to honouring. On Katz's terms the deployer has promised, through the machine, and the deeming runs back up a chain of authorization to a human. That isn't a refutation. It confirms that the speech act lives with whoever carries the debt.

**The weak form is the claim that we will be able to tell.** Katz offers this explicitly as a hypothesis he "as yet [has] no idea how to prove or disprove": that "there will always be something 'off' that humans can detect" ([Toward a Curriculum…](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy#p-14)). Here his own idiom works against him. He warns that "lists of things humans can do that machines can't merely provide a menu of AI improvements for the next generation of programmers to attempt" ([Thinking only through Models](/post/thinking-only-through-models#p-10)). He also writes that "the seemingly irresistible desire to insist upon some distinction between the human and the technological merely inspires someone to try and automate that distinctively human feature" ([Infra-Humaning](/post/infra-humaning#p-14)). A detectability claim is exactly that kind of menu item. He quickly relocates the stakes: these revisions of the Turing test "only really matter insofar as they provide models for performing our relations to the scenes we are on" (#p-15). In other words, the point is to promise and deem more explicitly ourselves, not to win the test.

**One real pressure point** is the case of systems that hold stakes. Katz discusses "agentic protocols" with their own tokens, cash flows and collateral ([Brute Force Computation](/post/brute-force-computation-and-the-debt-to-the-center#p-13)). If a system can post collateral and be liquidated, can it be held to a promise? On his logic I think the answer is still no, because the enforceability is chartered and guaranteed by human authority and the nomos. But the line becomes institutional rather than metaphysical. That makes it contingent on how those institutions are designed, and Katz would probably accept that.

## Next reading

- [Promise, Fraud, the Options on the Imperative, Messiah](/post/promise-fraud-the-options-on-the-imperative-messiah): his fullest account of the promise as debt and as the "most originary condition" of speech.
- [Toward a Curriculum for the New Officer Class Academy](/post/toward-a-curriculum-for-the-new-officer-class-academy): the deeming argument in its context of training people to issue rulings.

As an exercise, take a sentence you would write today and rewrite it twice: once as a pure declarative, and once as a promise or a ruling you could be held to. Then ask what in the second version would have to exist on the scene for it to bind: a creditor, an enforcer, a precedent. That list is Katz's answer to your question.

rows.q: Is singularized succession in perpetuity just monarchism? Give the strongest version of that objection and then Katz's reply.
rows.a:
## The objection at full strength

Put as hard as possible, the charge runs like this. Singularized succession in perpetuity (SSIP) is monarchism under a technical-sounding name. Three things support it.

**Katz's own account of where the idea came from.** He says the concept "was a continuation of the absolutist thinking through which I transitioned out of liberalism," starting from the maxim "that sovereignty is conserved," and concluding that "the most certain test that power was in fact held was that the sovereign selected his successor" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-1)).

**His explicit statements.** "It is true that monarchy is the only real form of governance—everything else is either mimicking monarchy or predicated on the endless struggle to prevent others from installing 'their' king" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-1)). Elsewhere he happily adopts "dictator" as the "perfect term" for the occupant of the center ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-1)).

**The structure of the concept.** One person sits at the center and names his heir. The rule of law cannot bind that choice: SSIP "completely invalidates the 'rule of law'" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). Every other value goes into it as well: "there is nothing more to governance than singularized succession in perpetuity," and consent, natural right and the common good are "either dispensed with or subsumed within it" ([Nomos and Transfer Translation](/post/nomos-and-transfer-translation#p-1)).

From these three points the critic draws a conclusion. If the chooser is single, unaccountable to law, and decides who comes next, that is a king. The word "perpetuity" only names the dynasty. And because the concept prizes continuity as such, it seems to bless whoever happens to hold power, including bad rulers.

## Katz's reply

Katz partly concedes this. He doesn't pretend SSIP is liberal; he calls it "the most anti or non-liberal concept possible." His reply is that "monarchism" is too narrow a name for what the concept does. He makes six moves.

**1. "Monarchy" is a placeholder.** In the same text where he calls monarchy the only real government, he goes straight on: "monarchy itself can take a lot of forms, so for the sake of inquiries into possibilities we need the concept of 'singular succession' to include all that we want in monarchy without restricting ourselves to forms of government 'similar' to known forms of monarchy" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-1)). His example is a data-security firm that gradually takes over the functions of sovereignty. Its CEO need not be a king. Monarchy is "still indispensable in arguing with 'democrats'," but "we're in uncharted waters" ([p-4](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4)).

**2. It cuts against heredity, which is the core of historical monarchy.** The concept "cuts against, without excluding, the most historically 'popular' means of monarchical succession, primogeniture, since succession is now understood as the outcome of competition and mentorship" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-2)). The designation can also be revoked at any time. Katz imagines a whole continuum of hand-offs, up to "rapid transfers of power from one figure to another... much like one might see in a baseball game a succession of relief pitchers" ([Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power#p-4)). He even says that, once losing power no longer means death, SSIP comes close to its apparent opposite, sortition: "anyone might give ruling a try for a bit" ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-12)). A crown passed by blood does neither of these things.

**3. "In perpetuity" turns the question into pedagogy, not dynasty.** The test is not who is best now. It is "the best person who will also be best in choosing a successor, seeing to all the conditions enabling that successor, who will best choose his successor, and so on" ([The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). Because no one can foresee the nth successor, the ruler's real work becomes "the intelligence infrastructures that make consistency and continuity more likely" ([p-5](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-5)). In practice that means schools, academies, apprenticeship and competition. The whole social order is reorganized around producing candidates. That is a theory of what society is for, and a theory of who sits on a throne would not need it.

**4. It is a description before it is a program, and it scales down to every practice.** Katz wants his concepts "descriptive and constitutive at the same time." Here: "a flawed society is one in which succession is not attended to... and a pathological society is one in which succession is actually subverted" ([The Sufficiency...](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-13)). The claim is that everyone with authority is already trying to "bias" the future toward people who will carry on their work. The left, he notes, "understand[s] succession far better than the right side of liberalism" ([Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-4)). The concept applies to the workshop as much as to the state: "you could define a practice in terms of the singularization of the one who will succeed it" ([Originary Technics](/post/originary-technics#p-27)). On this reading, monarchy is the case where the general structure is easiest to see.

**5. It selects among regimes without being one.** SSIP is formal. It "does not exclude any particular basis for social order" (ethnic or associative, traditionalist or experimental), but it "provide[s] a powerful principle of selection of one over another" ([The Sufficiency...](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-10)). It therefore works as a test you can put to any program, including Christian nationalism or Faustianism: "how does [it] identify and reach for the levers that would increase the likelihood of a singularized power center that would see to its own succession in perpetuity?" ([Staged Succession](/post/staged-succession-marginalizing-the-victimary-and-scapegoating-in-a-single-move#p-15)). In that sense it "situates all specific programs for appropriating power, without usurping any of them" ([p-17](/post/staged-succession-marginalizing-the-victimary-and-scapegoating-in-a-single-move#p-17)).

**6. Bad rulers, and the juridical.** To the question "do you want Biden to be allowed to choose his successor?" Katz answers that a weak occupant can't actually do it: "the successor such an occupant selects would not, in fact, succeed. Only someone who has the necessary threads tied up in his hands would dare" ([The Sufficiency...](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity#p-7)). Being able to name a successor is a measure of whether real power is held at all, not something given to whoever holds office. The ruler is also not beyond judgment. Katz imagines suits brought against the "dictator," with the possibility of countersuits. These make accusation costly without making it impossible, and they internalize the threat of civil war much as the party system once did ([Rotating Dictatorship](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-16)).

## Where the objection still lands

If "monarchism" means a single, final locus of command, with no liberal checks and continuity valued above consent, then Katz accepts the label and argues that every functioning order already works this way. If it means a hereditary, sacralized throne, he rejects it. He holds that sacral kingship cannot be restored; the point is to do what it did, joining the signifying and the occupied center, by other means. The real disagreement is whether that final locus of command can be made safe. Katz bets on pedagogy, staged and public competition among candidates, and juridical risk. A liberal would answer that those safeguards depend on the ruler's goodwill. The archive doesn't fully settle that question, and you can press it.

**Try it on a small case.** Take a founder of a company or a school. What would "succession in perpetuity" ask of her that "choose a good replacement" does not? Your answer will show you how far the concept is really about kings.

**Read next:**
- [The Sufficiency of Singularized Succession in Perpetuity](/post/the-sufficiency-of-singularized-succession-in-perpetuity): the fullest defense, including the bad-ruler question.
- [Continuum of Power](/post/continuum-of-power): the most direct place where Katz separates SSIP from known forms of monarchy.

rows.q: Take the essays on Judaism as a civilizational blockchain. What is the argument, and how does it follow from the originary hypothesis?
rows.a:
## The argument in brief

The essay [Judaism as Civilizational Blockchain](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain) is the third in a short series, after [A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism) and [A Bit More Granularity for a Cybernetics of Judaism and Thirdness](/post/a-bit-more-granularity-for-a-cybernetics-of-judaism-and-thirdness). Behind all three stands [The Longest, Most Convoluted, Revised and Thickly Imagined Title Deed Possible](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack). Together they make three moves.

**1. Hostility to Jews is a structure of attention, not just a prejudice.** Katz begins with how that hostility reasons: "The existence of Jews is a scandal, and therefore their existence is an unmistakable sign of immeasurable and monstrous Jewish power" ([p-1](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-1)). If Jews control the system, then the system cannot remedy the grievance. So "erasing the scandal of the Jews requires operating extra-juridically, even extra-systemically" ([p-2](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-2)). Followed to its end, the logic becomes "you must hunt the Jews or be hunted yourself as a Jew," and evidence turns into "ever fluctuating metrics of loyalty" ([p-19](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-19)). He calls this a comprehensive vendetta.

**2. The Jewish vocation is therefore the opposite of the vendetta.** If the enemy's project is to step outside judgment, the Jewish task is "maintaining all the institutional means of deferring vendetta" ([p-6](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-6)). Katz takes up the old claim that being Jewish means witnessing to injustice ([p-9](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-9)). He narrows it sharply. It is not leftist "social injustice." It is the working of the juridical inside the terms of the nomos, meaning the founding distribution of property and standing that every lawsuit refers back to. Hence the formula: Jews "should try to become a civilizational blockchain—recording social exchanges and disputes as objectively and permanently as we can" ([p-11](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-11)).

**3. This fits what Judaism already is.** "The blockchain is where covenants can be recorded in a permanent, inalterable manner" ([p-12](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-12)). Katz follows Bernard Lamborelle's hypothesis that the original covenant was a land grant from a Mesopotamian king, later raised into a covenant with God. On that reading, Jews "are better thought of as a nation of scribes than a nation of priests" ([p-13](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-13)). The Cybernetics essay puts it more starkly: "A nation of priests became a nation of scribes which means a nation of ledgerers" ([p-6](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-6)). The title-deed essay reads the whole Hebrew Bible as the record of a deed passed down through disputed inheritances. Every layer had to be kept because "it preserved indispensable evidence of the continuity of the transmission of the deed" ([p-10](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack#p-10)).

Note one thing Katz is clear about: the blockchain role "involves exercising power" ([p-15](/post/judaism-as-civilizational-blockchain#p-15)). It is not victimhood. The companion essay names the aim directly: "the historical responsibility of the Jews is to make governance good" ([p-8](/post/a-bit-more-granularity-for-a-cybernetics-of-judaism-and-thirdness#p-8)).

## How it follows from the originary hypothesis

The links run through four concepts.

**Deferral, scaled up.** On the originary scene, the members of the group converge on a shared object and violence is imminent. The sign turns that rush into a shared, deferred attention. For Katz the juridical is the same gesture at imperial scale. Judges and administrators exist "to keep the vendetta at bay, both from below (tribal conflicts) and from above (systemic resentments instrumentalized by a section of the governing class)" ([Rotating Dictatorship, p-19](/post/rotating-dictatorship#p-19)). A ledger of disputes is deferral made permanent. It lets a conflict be referred to a center rather than settled by one party's force. The Cybernetics essay even defines God in these terms: "God’s voice is whatever tells us when and how to defer violence, or when and how we are failing to do so" ([p-9](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism#p-9)).

**The scapegoat as convergence on a false center.** The antisemitic structure in step 1 is mimetic crisis in its classic form. All resentment converges on one figure, imagined as the hidden power behind the visible center. Katz argues elsewhere that scapegoating always targets the center through someone presumed to be "behind the scenes." The fantasy of total Jewish control is exactly that. So the remedy cannot be a counter-narrative, since that is just another myth. The remedy is a more transparent center, where power is legible and grievances can be heard.

**The nomos and originary debt.** The originary scene ends in a distribution: the shared meal, and later the division of land after conquest. Every later claim refers back to that distribution. A title deed carried across three millennia is the nomos remembered with unusual stubbornness. Keeping that record is, in Katz's terms, a way of paying the debt to the center.

**Memory and commemoration.** The sign has to be repeated to mean anything, and the scene has to be remembered to hold. Scribal culture, a text revised but never discarded, is a technology of that repetition. "Blockchain" is simply Katz's current idiom for it, and it carries his later vocabulary of data exchange and the stack.

## What to read next

- [The Longest, Most Convoluted, Revised and Thickly Imagined Title Deed Possible](/post/the-longest-most-convoluted-revised-and-thickly-imagined-title-deed-possible-substack) gives the full scriptural argument the blockchain essay assumes.
- [A Cybernetics of Judaism](/post/a-cybernetics-of-judaism) shows how the "ledgerer" role ties to persecution, empire, and Katz's proposal that Jews read their persecutions as lessons in failed deferral.

A question to take further: Katz claims the juridical "can always collapse back into" the vendetta. What would it look like for a community's record-keeping to become partisan, a vendetta conducted by other means? And what in the originary scene suggests how to prevent that?
